The story

Founded in 1848 by Louis Brandt in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, the company initially assembled pocket watches. His sons, Louis-Paul and César Brandt, later moved the business to Biel/Bienne and transitioned to in-house manufacturing. A pivotal moment came in 1894 with the introduction of the 19-ligne “Omega” caliber, a movement so successful for its precision and interchangeable parts that the company was renamed the Omega Watch Co. in 1903. Omega's reputation for precision led to its selection as the official timekeeper for the Olympic Games in 1932. The post-war era saw the launch of some of its most enduring collections. The Seamaster debuted in 1948, building on the brand's experience with military watches. This was followed by the Constellation in 1952, which became a symbol of chronometric precision. In 1957, Omega introduced the Speedmaster, originally designed for sports and racing, which would later become the first watch worn on the Moon during the Apollo 11 mission in 1969. The elegant De Ville, initially part of the Seamaster line in the early 1960s, became its own collection in 1967. The brand also produced specialized models like the Flightmaster for pilots, introduced in 1969. In 1999, Omega introduced the first mass-produced watch with the revolutionary Co-Axial escapement, a significant innovation in mechanical watchmaking. Today, Omega continues to be a leading name in the watch industry as part of the Swatch Group. It is known for its advanced anti-magnetic materials and the Master Chronometer certification, which signifies a high standard of precision and performance across its collections, including modern interpretations of the Seamaster Diver 300M, the Seamaster Planet Ocean 600M, and various Speedmaster models like the Speedmaster Professional.
